record.question: What project oversight services does OCERS require from the consultant in its 2023 RFP for Pension Administration Project Oversight and Consultation Services?
record.answer:
# Markdown Briefing: OCERS 2023 RFP Project Oversight Services for PAS

## Overview
OCERS requires the consultant to serve as an **on-site, full-time project oversight and implementation partner** for the selection and implementation of a new **Pension Administration Solution (PAS)**. The consultant’s role extends beyond advisory support to include **central project oversight, quality assurance, vendor management, governance, reporting, and post-go-live support** over an expected **three-year implementation**.

## Core Required Services

### 1. Project Oversight and Management
- Provide **overall project management and quality oversight** for the PAS selection and implementation.
- Help OCERS manage the project to ensure it meets **requirements, schedule, and budget**.
- Coordinate with OCERS’ **Enterprise Project Management Office (EPMO)**.

### 2. Planning and Early Project Development
- Support **requirements definition**, **solution design**, and **IT strategic roadmap planning**.
- Conduct **needs and requirements assessments**.
- Develop:
  - **staffing plan**
  - **IT Strategic Roadmap**
  - **implementation project plan**
  - **overall implementation approach**
- Identify **milestones** and **resource needs**.

### 3. Procurement and RFP Support
- Draft and manage **RFP(s)** for PAS software and related services.
- Coordinate procurement with OCERS staff.
- Support vendor evaluation and final selection through:
  - software demonstrations
  - vendor interviews
  - **BAFO** review
  - contract review

### 4. Vendor Coordination and Implementation Oversight
- Oversee **design, development, testing, training, and implementation**.
- Ensure vendors satisfy **RFP requirements** and the **requirements matrix**.
- Coordinate across OCERS functions, including **Procurement, Legal, IT, and Member Services**.
- Support **data cleansing, migration, and conversion strategy**.

### 5. Governance and Change Control
- Establish **sign-off procedures** across the system development life cycle.
- Ensure **change control procedures** are followed.
- Ensure schedule changes are properly reflected in project plans.

### 6. Deliverables, Documentation, and Budget Control
- Review and manage major project deliverables and documentation, including:
  - statements of work
  - task descriptions
  - data conversion and reconciliation plans
  - test plans, scripts, and cases
  - user acceptance plans and criteria
  - cutover plans and schedules
- Help establish **requirements-gathering procedures**.
- Manage the **project budget**.

### 7. Risk, Issue, Methodology, and Quality Management
- Ensure a **rigorous project methodology**, planning framework, and schedule discipline.
- Manage **issues, escalations, and resolutions**.
- Identify and manage **project risks**.
- Develop **testing procedures** to support quality assurance.
- Address project management issues that may threaten project success.

### 8. Reporting and Stakeholder Communication
- Provide **project reports, metrics, and due-date tracking**.
- Prepare and present a **monthly oversight status report** to:
  - the **Steering Committee**
  - the **OCERS Board of Retirement**
- Provide updates to **external stakeholders** and facilitate related meetings.

### 9. Organizational Change Management and Training
- Help lead **organizational change management (OCM)**.
- Support and oversee **staff training** throughout implementation.

### 10. Strategic and Future-State Alignment
- Incorporate OCERS strategic goals, including future readiness for:
  - **RPA**
  - **Machine Learning**
  - **Artificial Intelligence**
- Help define a **future-proof solution** that supports growth and integration.
- Establish a **common glossary of terms** across project teams.

### 11. Post-Implementation Support
- Provide **post-go-live support**, with final scope and duration to be agreed upon later.

## Delivery Expectations
- **On-site delivery**
- **Full-time engagement**
- Expected start: **around February 2024**
- Estimated duration: **approximately three years**

## Bottom Line
OCERS expects the consultant to function as the **primary oversight, governance, and quality-assurance partner** across the full PAS lifecycle: **planning, procurement, vendor selection, implementation, testing, training, reporting, change management, and post-implementation support**.

description: OCERS’ 2023 RFP requires the consultant to provide on-site project oversight and consultation for the selection and implementation of a new Pension Administration Solution (PAS). The work centers on project management oversight, quality assurance, procurement and RFP support, vendor coordination, reporting, risk and issue management, change control, testing, training, and post-implementation support.
cluster.content:
In its 2023 RFP, OCERS requires the consultant to act as an implementation partner and oversight project manager for its pension administration project, with the goal of helping OCERS select, implement, and successfully deploy a new Pension Administration Solution (PAS) to replace its current system.

Key required project oversight services include:

1. Overall project oversight and management
- Provide project management and quality oversight for the full PAS selection and implementation effort.
- Assist OCERS in actively managing and overseeing the implementation process through review, facilitation, guidance, and staff support.
- Help ensure the new system meets project requirements, stays on schedule, and remains within budget.
- Coordinate with OCERS’ Enterprise Project Management Office (EPMO).

2. Planning and early project development
- Coordinate planning tasks tied to:
  - requirements definition,
  - IT strategic roadmap development,
  - solution design.
- Perform a needs and requirements assessment.
- Create a staffing plan.
- Create an IT Strategic Roadmap plan.
- Develop the PAS implementation project plan and overall implementation approach.
- Identify project milestones and resource needs throughout the project.

3. Procurement and RFP development support
- Write the RFP(s) for required software applications and/or related services.
- Prepare concise and comprehensive RFP(s) for the new PAS.
- Coordinate the procurement process with OCERS staff.
- Support review and selection of the winning solution.
- Facilitate competitive procurement activities such as:
  - software demonstrations,
  - vendor interviews,
  - evaluation of BAFO submissions,
  - final vendor selection.
- Review PAS vendor contracts.

4. Vendor coordination and implementation oversight
- Coordinate and oversee PAS design, development, testing, training, and implementation activities.
- Ensure software vendor(s) satisfy all RFP requirements and have an approach or strategy to address each requirement.
- Coordinate and manage vendors.
- Ensure vendors meet the requirements matrix.
- Work cooperatively with OCERS staff, including Procurement, Legal, IT, and Member Services.
- Work with OCERS and PAS vendor(s) on the overall conversion strategy, including:
  - data cleansing,
  - data migration,
  - data conversion.

5. Governance and sign-off controls
- Establish and ensure adequate sign-off procedures throughout the system development life cycle.
- Ensure change control procedures are followed.
- Ensure project schedule changes are properly reflected in the project plan.

6. Deliverables, documentation, and controls
- Develop, review, and comment on all major project deliverables and documentation.
- Coordinate and manage deliverables including:
  - statements of work and task descriptions,
  - data conversion plans and reconciliation procedures,
  - system test plans, scripts, and cases,
  - user acceptance plan and acceptance criteria,
  - project schedule and cutover plans, including timelines and process.
- Manage the project budget.
- Work with OCERS and the PAS vendor to establish procedures for requirements gathering.

7. Methodology, communications, issues, risks, and quality
- Ensure a rigorous project methodology, planning structure, and schedule are proposed and followed.
- Ensure project issues and status are properly communicated.
- Ensure project issues are properly managed, escalated when necessary, and resolved in a timely manner.
- Identify and address project risks for proper management.
- Develop testing procedures to ensure the highest level of quality.
- Address any other project management issues that could hinder successful completion.

8. Reporting and stakeholder communication
- Provide project management reports and metrics for accurate status and due-date reporting to key participants.
- Prepare a monthly oversight status report.
- Present the monthly status report to both:
  - the Steering Committee,
  - the OCERS Board of Retirement.
- Provide project updates to external stakeholders as requested by the Steering Committee.
- Facilitate meetings and implementation oversight activities with external stakeholders such as employers and third-party vendors.

9. Organizational change management and training
- Help lead Organizational Change Management (OCM) efforts.
- Support staff training on the PAS throughout the project.
- Oversee training activities as part of implementation.

10. Strategic and future-state considerations
- Incorporate OCERS strategic initiatives into the PAS effort, including movement toward:
  - Robotic Process Automation (RPA),
  - Machine Learning (ML),
  - Artificial Intelligence.
- Help create a future-proof solution capable of growth and integration with current and emerging technologies.
- Agree on a glossary of terms for consistent communication across project teams.

11. Post-implementation support
- Provide post-implementation support, with the final scope and duration to be mutually agreed upon with the selected vendor.

12. Delivery model
- The services must be provided on-site.
- OCERS envisions the engagement as full-time.
- The implementation is expected to begin around February 2024 and take about three years.

In short, OCERS is seeking a consultant not just to advise, but to serve as the central oversight and quality-assurance partner across planning, procurement, implementation, governance, reporting, vendor management, change management, and post-go-live support for the new PAS.

Pension Administration System Consulting RFP Page 3
Section 1: Introduction
The Orange County Employees Retirement System (“OCERS”) is requesting proposals from qualified 
firms interested in providing consulting services to aid in the design, selection of, and smooth 
implementation of their new Pension Administration Solution (PAS). This solution will replace their 
current system, V3. The selected consultant will be responsible for providing Oversight Project 
Management services, which will include staff support and quality assurance. These services are vital to 
support the successful implementation of the new PAS. It's worth noting that the selection of the new 
PAS will be made independently of, but simultaneously with, the selection of the implementation 
consultant.
The project's expected start date is approximately February 2024, and the entire PAS implementation 
process is estimated to take around 3 years to complete. OCERS envisions this as a full-time consulting 
engagement.
The primary role of the selected consultant will be to assist OCERS in efficiently managing and 
overseeing the implementation process. This involves active participation, careful review, facilitation, 
and guidance throughout the project. The consultant's goal is to ensure that the new system fulfills all 
project requirements, is completed within the designated timeframe, and remains within the allocated 
budget. The solution may include multiple software solutions that will need to interact with each other. 
Our intention is to have a future proof solution with the ability to grow and incorporate current and 
emerging technologies such as Intelligent Automation.
Questions about this RFP must be submitted in writing by 5:00 p.m., PT, Friday, September 29 to Jim 
Doezie, Contracts, Risk & Performance Administrator, by email at jdoezie@ocers.org or direct to 
Planetbids through this link: https://pbsystem.planetbids.com/portal/56826/bo/bo-detail/109932
Those who wish to be considered must submit their completed proposal by 5:00 p.m., PT, Friday, 
October 20, 2023. Specific instructions for proposal submissions are contained in Section 7 of this RFP. 
Section 2: Background
OCERS was established in 1945 under the County Employees Retirement Law of 1937, providing
members with retirement, disability, death, and cost-of-living benefits. There are approximately 50,000 
members served by OCERS, of which over 19,000 are retirees. OCERS is governed by a nine-member 
Board of Retirement (“Board”), which has plenary authority and fiduciary responsibility for the 
investment of moneys and administration of the retirement system. OCERS has over one hundred 
employees, and the Board appoints a Chief Executive Officer responsible for the agency’s management. 
For additional information about OCERS, please refer to the OCERS website at ocers.org.
Section 3: Scope of Services
The detailed scope of services for this engagement is outlined in the attached Exhibit “B” (“Scope of 
Services”). The primary objectives are to provide OCERS with guidance and project management
oversight in selecting and implementing a new PAS.
The firm selected for this engagement will be expected to meet requirements that include, but are not 
limited to, the following:

Pension Administration System Consulting RFP Page 4
1. The firm must have all necessary permits and licenses to perform the requested services and 
must be bonded where applicable. 
2. Minimum insurance coverage must include the following items, and proof of such insurance 
must be provided to OCERS prior to the commencement of work, on an annual basis, and upon 
request: 
• Commercial General Liability: $2M per occurrence, $2M aggregate
• Automobile Liability: $1M per occurrence, $2M aggregate
• Workers Compensation: $1M per occurrence, $1M aggregate
• Umbrella Liability: $5M per occurrence, $5M aggregate 
• Professional Liability: $2M per occurrence, $3M aggregate
OCERS must be listed as an additional insured on the above policies.
3. The firm shall provide all personnel, equipment, tools, materials, vehicles, supervision, and 
other items and services necessary to perform all services, tasks, and functions as requested in 
this RFP. 
4. The initial term of the contract awarded pursuant to this RFP will be for a three-year period,
with OCERS retaining the option to renew the contract, on an annual basis, for up to an 
additional three years. The total term of the contract will not exceed six years. 
5. All work under the contract awarded shall be performed and all equipment furnished or 
installed in accordance with applicable safety codes, ordinances, and other regulations, 
including the regulations of the State of California, Division of Industrial Safety and the 
provisions of the California Labor Code.
6. Minimum Qualifications 
All respondents are required to sign and return the “Minimum Qualifications Certification,”
attached as Exhibit “B.” 
Section 4: General Conditions
All terms, conditions, requirements, and procedures included in this RFP must be met for a proposal to 
be qualified. A proposal that fails to meet any material term, condition, requirement, or procedure of 
this RFP may be disqualified. OCERS reserves the right to waive or permit the cure of non-material errors 
or omissions. OCERS reserves the right to modify, amend, or cancel the terms of this RFP at any time. 
OCERS may modify this RFP before the date fixed for submission of a proposal by posting, mailing, 
emailing, or faxing an addendum to the respondents known to be interested in submitting a proposal.
However, failure of a respondent to receive or acknowledge receipt of any addendum shall not relieve 
the respondent of the responsibility for complying with the terms thereof.
A respondent’s proposal shall constitute an irrevocable offer for the 120 days following the deadline for 
submission of proposals. Reference to a certain number of days in this RFP shall mean calendar days 
unless otherwise specified.

Pension Administration System Consulting RFP Page 5
All proposals submitted in response to this RFP will become the exclusive property of OCERS. Therefore, 
proposals will not be returned to respondents.
By submitting a proposal, the respondent acknowledges that it has read this RFP, understands it, and 
agrees to be bound by its requirements unless clearly and specifically noted in the proposal submitted.
Section 5: Point of Contact
A quiet period will be in effect from the date of issuance of this RFP until announcement of the 
candidate(s) selected. During the quiet period, respondents are not permitted to communicate with any 
OCERS staff member or Board Member regarding this RFP except through the Point of Contact named 
herein. Respondents violating this quiet period may be disqualified at OCERS’ discretion. In addition, 
respondents having current business with OCERS must limit their communications to the subject of such 
business. 
OCERS’ regular business hours are from 08:00 to 17:00, Monday through Friday, except for federal and 
state holidays.
The Point of Contact for all matters relating to this RFP is:
Name: Jim Doezie
Title: Contracts, Risk & Performance Administrator

items can also be found here: 
http://www.ocers.org/rfp/requestforproposal.htm

Pension Administration System Consulting RFP Page 6
Section 6: Response to Request for Proposal
Proposals must be submitted to the Point of Contact identified in Section 5 and delivered by the due 
date and time stated below in the RFP Schedule. 
OCERS will accept electronic, submissions either direct or via Planetbids. Proposals may be submitted 
electronically in Microsoft Word or Adobe Acrobat PDF format to the email address noted in Section 5.
The Planetbids link is: https://pbsystem.planetbids.com/portal/56826/bo/bo-detail/109932
RFP Schedule
The following timetable constitutes a tentative schedule for this RFP process. OCERS reserves the 
right to modify this schedule at any time.
Deliverable Date Time
Release of RFP 9/21/2023 5:00 p.m. PT
RFP Questions Deadline 9/29/2023 5:00 p.m. PT
RFP Answers Posted 10/06/2023 5:00 p.m. PT
RFP Submission Deadline 10/20/2023 5:00 p.m. PT
OCERS Review of RFP Submissions 11/13/2023
Selection of Finalists 11/15/2023
Interviews of Finalists 11/16/2023 – 12/08/2023
Service Award [or recommendation to the Board] 12/15/2023
Section 7: Proposal Requirements
Proposals must include the following information:
1. The “Minimum Qualifications Certification,” attached as Exhibit “B.”
2. The “Proposal Cover Page and Check List,” attached as Exhibit “C.”
3. An executive summary that provides the respondent’s background, experience, and other 
qualifications to provide the services included in the Scope of Services. 
4. A description of the respondent including:
a. Brief history, including year the respondent firm was formed.
b. Ownership structure.
c. Office locations.
d. Organization chart.

Pension Administration System Consulting RFP Page 7
e. Number of employees.
f. Annual revenues.
g. Scope of services offered.
h. Respondent’s specialties, strengths, and limitations.
i. The average retention rate (years of service) of the firm’s other clients? 
5. The names and qualifications of the staff that will be assigned to OCERS work, including a 
detailed profile of each person’s background and relevant individual experience. 
6. At least three (3) references for which the respondent has provided services like those included 
in the Scope of Services. Please include for each reference the individual point of contact, a 
summary of the work performed, and the length of time the respondent provided each service.
7. Copies of any pertinent licenses required to deliver respondent’s product or service (e.g.,
business license).
8. An explanation of the pricing proposal for the scope of work, including pricing of fees and costs, 
billing practices, and payment terms that would apply. OCERS does limit the pricing approach to 
pricing and will consider alternative pricing methods for the scope of work, or portions of it. This 
section of the response should include an explanation as to how the pricing approach(es) will be 
managed to provide the best value to OCERS. The respondent should represent that the pricing 
offered to OCERS is, and will remain, equivalent to or better than that provided to other public 
pension fund or institutional investor clients or explain why this representation cannot be 
provided. All pricing proposals should be “best and final,” although OCERS reserves the right to 
negotiate on pricing.
9. An explanation of all actual or potential conflicts of interest that the respondent may have in 
contracting with OCERS. 
10. A description of all past, pending, or threatened litigation, including malpractice claims, 
administrative, state ethics, disciplinary proceedings, and other claims against respondent
and/or any of the individuals proposed to provide services to OCERS.
11. Any other information that the respondent deems relevant to OCERS’ selection process.
Section 8: Evaluation Criteria
Responses will be evaluated based upon the following: 
1. Experience and reputation of the respondent. 
2. Quality of the team proposed to provide services to OCERS, including staffing depth, 
experience, turnover, and compensation. 
3. Pricing and value. 
4. Delivery and payment terms.
5. Compliance with technical standards contained in this RFP.
6. The organization, completeness, and quality of the proposal.
7. Information provided by references.
8. Other factors OCERS determines to be relevant.

Pension Administration System Consulting RFP Page 8
The factors will be considered as a whole, without a specific weighting.
OCERS may require one or more interviews with or personal presentations by finalists to be 
conducted with staff or members of the Board of Retirement. 
If the proposal’s information is deemed to be insufficient for evaluation, OCERS may request additional 
information or reject the proposal outright at OCERS’ sole discretion. In addition, false, incomplete, or 
unresponsive statements in connection with a proposal may result in rejection of the proposal.
Section 9: Non-Discrimination Requirement
By submitting a proposal, the respondent represents that it and its subsidiaries do not and will not 
discriminate against any employee or applicant for employment based on race, religion, color, national

Section 1: Introduction
The Orange County Employees Retirement System (“OCERS”) is requesting proposals from qualified 
firms interested in providing consulting services to aid in the design, selection of, and smooth 
implementation of their new Pension Administration Solution (PAS). This solution will replace their 
current system, V3. The selected consultant will be responsible for providing Oversight Project 
Management services, which will include staff support and quality assurance. These services are vital to 
support the successful implementation of the new PAS. It's worth noting that the selection of the new 
PAS will be made independently of, but simultaneously with, the selection of the implementation 
consultant.
The project's expected start date is approximately February 2024, and the entire PAS implementation 
process is estimated to take around 3 years to complete. OCERS envisions this as a full-time consulting 
engagement.
The primary role of the selected consultant will be to assist OCERS in efficiently managing and 
overseeing the implementation process. This involves active participation, careful review, facilitation, 
and guidance throughout the project. The consultant's goal is to ensure that the new system fulfills all 
project requirements, is completed within the designated timeframe, and remains within the allocated 
budget. The solution may include multiple software solutions that will need to interact with each other. 
Our intention is to have a future proof solution with the ability to grow and incorporate current and 
emerging technologies such as Intelligent Automation.
Questions about this RFP must be submitted in writing by 5:00 p.m., PT, Friday, September 29 to Jim 
Doezie, Contracts, Risk & Performance Administrator, by email at jdoezie@ocers.org or direct to 
Planetbids through this link: https://pbsystem.planetbids.com/portal/56826/bo/bo-detail/109932
Those who wish to be considered must submit their completed proposal by 5:00 p.m., PT, Friday, 
October 20, 2023. Specific instructions for proposal submissions are contained in Section 7 of this RFP. 
Section 2: Background
OCERS was established in 1945 under the County Employees Retirement Law of 1937, providing
members with retirement, disability, death, and cost-of-living benefits. There are approximately 50,000 
members served by OCERS, of which over 19,000 are retirees. OCERS is governed by a nine-member 
Board of Retirement (“Board”), which has plenary authority and fiduciary responsibility for the 
investment of moneys and administration of the retirement system. OCERS has over one hundred 
employees, and the Board appoints a Chief Executive Officer responsible for the agency’s management. 
For additional information about OCERS, please refer to the OCERS website at ocers.org.

Pension Administration Project Oversight
OCERS is seeking an implementation partner for this mission critical pension 
administration project. The service required consists of developing and reviewing key 
project management deliverables to ensure that the following are being properly 
addressed:
1. Planning – Coordinating tasks associated with requirements definition, IT strategic 
roadmap, and solutions design.
2. Writing the RFP(s) for the required software applications and/or services. 
3. Coordinate for the procurement process for review and selection of winning
solution with OCERS staff. Additional in-depth details are listed under the 
“Selection and Implementation of New PAS” section.
4. Oversight of New PAS: Coordinate the design, development, testing, and training 
and implementation activities. Ensure that the software vendor(s) satisfies all 
items as listed in the RFP and has an approach/strategy in place to address each 
item as stated. Coordinate with OCERS’ Enterprise Project Management Office 
(EPMO).
5. Establish Sign-Off Process – Ensure that adequate sign-off procedures are 
followed throughout the system development life cycle.
6. Project Deliverables – Provide project management reports and metrics for 
accurate status and due-date reporting to key participants. Develop, review and 
comment on all project deliverables, documentation, etc., e.g.:
• Perform a needs and requirements assessment
• Create a staffing plan
• Create an IT Strategic Roadmap plan
• Manage the project budget
• Coordinate and manage vendors
• Ensure vendors meet the requirements matrix
• Coordination of the following:
• Statement of Work and Task Descriptions
• Data conversion plans and reconciliation procedures
• System test plans, scripts, cases, etc.
• User acceptance plan, acceptance criteria, etc.
• Project Schedule including cutover plans: timelines 
and process
7. Project Methodology, Planning and Scheduling – Ensure that a rigorous methodology,

schedule are properly reflected in the project plan.
8. Project Communications – Ensure that project issues and status are properly
communicated.

properly escalated and addressed in a timely manner.
10. Project Risk – Identify and address project risk for proper management.
11. Change Control – Ensure that change control procedures are followed.
12. Quality – Develop testing procedures to ensure the highest level of quality.
13. Consider and address other project management issues that might hinder successful 
completion of the project.

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the 
following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment 
performance history.
F. Manager Guidelines:
1. Managers shall have full discretionary authority in the selection 
and retention of investments, subject to the provision of law, trust 
agreements, this Statement of Investment Policy as amended from 
time to time and investment management agreement between the 
System and the manager.
2. The responsibility for security selection shall lie with the managers.
The managers, however, shall operate within these investment 
guidelines which shall conform to applicable governmental 
regulations, and shall cover four specific areas: (a) diversification; 
(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.
a. Diversification:
(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the 
security’s weight in the agreed upon market index 
plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be 
requested as provided below in section (d).
(2) No security shall be bought unless it is traded on
one of the major security exchanges or the Over-The-Counter (OTC) market. Listed American
Depository Receipts (ADR’s) shall be an approved
investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a 
manager’s portfolio. The manager is required to provide
the Board with a list and explanation of the types of
derivatives they expect to invest in, the purposes for
holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a 
description of the risks associated with these 
investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

10
but individual issues must have a Flow Uncertainty
Index (“FLUX”) score of 15 or less.
b. Credit quality:
(1) Commercial paper must be rated P-1 and/or A-1 by
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s respectively.
(2) The total bond portfolio will maintain a minimum 
average credit rating of “BBB+” as rated by both 
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. For Purposes of
compliance with this Policy, the manager will 
adhere to the same ratings scale and policy as that 
employed by Bloomberg in the structure of the 
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (utilizing ratings by 
Moody’s, S & P and Fitch).
c. Portfolio Duration:
Total portfolio weighted average duration should not
exceed 120% of the bond market’s duration utilizing the
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index.
d. Restricted transactions:
(1) Conflict of interest and transactions between a
fiduciary and parties in interest, as described in
Sections 406 and 408 of Title I, Employee 
Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), are 
prohibited which provisions are adopted for use in 
this System.
(2) No transactions shall be made which might 
threaten the tax exempt status of the system.
(3) No letter stocks shall be purchased.
(4) No funds shall be borrowed.
(5) No short sales shall be made.
(6) No tax-exempt bond shall be purchased or retained
unless, on a comparable quality and duration basis, it
provides an expected return superior to that of a 
taxable bond.
(7) No private placements shall be purchased. 
However, Rule 144A securities with registration 
rights are permitted investments.
(8) No non-exchange-listed derivatives shall be
purchased or sold by any of the System’s managers.

11
e. Exceptions to Manager Guidelines:
(9) The Board acknowledges that when it is in the best
interests of the System to invest in a collective 
vehicle (i.e. comingled fund or mutual fund); it is 
not possible to dictate specific investment 
prohibitions. Therefore, it shall be the duty of the 
manager of such commingled fund to report to the 
Board on a periodic basis, the extent to which the 
investment strategies differ from the Board’s SIP.
Periodically, the Board will review the differences 
and determine if the commingled fund remains in 
the best interest of the System.
(10) The managers may request exceptions to the
restrictions outlined in V.F.2. by written
request to the Board.
(11) All exceptions will be submitted in writing to the
Board who will, after reviewing and receiving 
advice from the Fund’s Investment Consultant,
render a decision with regard to the request at the
next board meeting.
3. Brokerage Transactions
The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)
J. APPROVAL
This latest revision to the Statement of Investment Policy is approved by a super-majority vote of the Retirement Board at the meeting held on August 16, 2023.

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the 
following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment

F. Manager Guidelines:
1. Managers shall have full discretionary authority in the selection 
and retention of investments, subject to the provision of law, trust 
agreements, this Statement of Investment Policy as amended from 
time to time and investment management agreement between the 
System and the manager.
2. The responsibility for security selection shall lie with the managers.
The managers, however, shall operate within these investment 
guidelines which shall conform to applicable governmental 
regulations, and shall cover four specific areas: (a) diversification; 
(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.
a. Diversification:
(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the 
security’s weight in the agreed upon market index 
plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be 
requested as provided below in section (d).
(2) No security shall be bought unless it is traded on
one of the major security exchanges or the Over-The-Counter (OTC) market. Listed American
Depository Receipts (ADR’s) shall be an approved
investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a 
manager’s portfolio. The manager is required to provide
the Board with a list and explanation of the types of
derivatives they expect to invest in, the purposes for
holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a 
description of the risks associated with these 
investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

but individual issues must have a Flow Uncertainty
Index (“FLUX”) score of 15 or less.
b. Credit quality:
(1) Commercial paper must be rated P-1 and/or A-1 by
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s respectively.
(2) The total bond portfolio will maintain a minimum 
average credit rating of “BBB+” as rated by both 
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. For Purposes of
compliance with this Policy, the manager will 
adhere to the same ratings scale and policy as that 
employed by Bloomberg in the structure of the 
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (utilizing ratings by 
Moody’s, S & P and Fitch).
c. Portfolio Duration:
Total portfolio weighted average duration should not
exceed 120% of the bond market’s duration utilizing the
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index.
d. Restricted transactions:
(1) Conflict of interest and transactions between a
fiduciary and parties in interest, as described in
Sections 406 and 408 of Title I, Employee 
Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), are

(2) No transactions shall be made which might

However, Rule 144A securities with registration 
rights are permitted investments.
(8) No non-exchange-listed derivatives shall be
purchased or sold by any of the System’s managers.

11
e. Exceptions to Manager Guidelines:
(9) The Board acknowledges that when it is in the best
interests of the System to invest in a collective 
vehicle (i.e. comingled fund or mutual fund); it is 
not possible to dictate specific investment 
prohibitions. Therefore, it shall be the duty of the 
manager of such commingled fund to report to the 
Board on a periodic basis, the extent to which the 
investment strategies differ from the Board’s SIP.
Periodically, the Board will review the differences 
and determine if the commingled fund remains in 
the best interest of the System.
(10) The managers may request exceptions to the
restrictions outlined in V.F.2. by written
request to the Board.
(11) All exceptions will be submitted in writing to the
Board who will, after reviewing and receiving 
advice from the Fund’s Investment Consultant,
render a decision with regard to the request at the
next board meeting.
3. Brokerage Transactions
The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)
J. APPROVAL
This latest revision to the Statement of Investment Policy is approved by a super-majority vote of the Retirement Board at the meeting held on August 16, 2023. 
______________________ _______________________ 
 Date Chairperson

The Compass Fund seeks to provide an attractive yield, safety of principal and daily liquidity; under normal
